candidates.title: Physical siren is controlled by an unauthenticated topic on a public MQTT broker
candidates.description: The tracked config.yaml selects actuator type mqtt on the public broker broker.hivemq.com:1883 with topic guardian/demo7k3x9/siren and null credentials. The ESP32 firmware wokwi/sketch.ino hard-codes the same broker and topic, connects anonymously over plaintext TCP, and acts on every message on the topic without any sender identity, signature or freshness check. Because the device can only work on a broker that admits anonymous clients to this topic, any other anonymous client that knows or finds the topic string (it is literal in two tracked files) can do four things. (1) Publish ON:<n> to sound the siren and LED for an unbounded time: one ON:2592000 holds it about 30 days, and repeated messages extend it indefinitely. (2) Publish OFF, or WARN (which calls noTone), to silence a real ALTO alarm right after the backend's ON:10, which it can see by subscribing to the same topic. (3) Publish the command as retained, so the broker replays it each time the device reconnects. (4) Subscribe to learn in real time when the system raises MEDIO/ALTO alerts. settings.py lets the environment override only the MQTT username and password, never host or topic, and docker-compose.yml mounts the repository config.yaml read-only into backend and detector. Exploitability depends on the public broker's access policy and on whether a real device, not only the Wokwi simulation named in the sketch header, runs this firmware.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: Siren control has no producer authentication; the only control is a topic name on a shared public broker. Neither the producer connection (actuator.py MQTTActuator) nor the consumer connection (wokwi/sketch.ino connectMqtt) uses credentials or TLS, and the consumer (wokwi/sketch.ino onMessage) neither authenticates nor bounds commands.

candidates.title: All communities' private-camera alerts go to one global Telegram chat and siren, ignoring admin_can_view
candidates.description: Every MEDIO/ALTO event dispatched by the backend comes from a resident's own private camera: /ws/live and /analyze accept only the caller's private, active camera. dispatch_live_alert and dispatch_alerts receive only the event dict (image name, level, score, reasons) and send it to a process-wide dispatcher built once from config.yaml/env: one MQTT siren topic, one Telegram bot and chat_id, one zone name. The event's community, camera owner and admin_can_view flag are never consulted. The web application hides a private camera's events and evidence from the community admin when admin_can_view is false, audits admin views, and tells the owner 'the community administrator cannot see this camera and its events'. Yet the Telegram path posts that camera's evidence frame to the configured chat with no visibility check and no audit. It also labels every alert with the single configured zone ('Cuadra 01 - Piloto') and fires the single siren for events from any community. The schema's per-user and per-community notification_channels (with min_level) and alert_deliveries show that per-tenant routing was intended but is not implemented. If the chat includes anyone other than the trusted operator (for example the pilot community's admin or neighbours), residents of every community, including those who hid their camera from the admin, have their private-camera frames disclosed to that chat. Residents of other communities also sound the pilot site's siren.

candidates.title: Global per-level live alert cooldown lets one user's events suppress other users' and communities' alerts
candidates.description: dispatch_live_alert keeps one module-level _last_alert dict keyed only by level ('MEDIO'/'ALTO'). It returns early whenever the same level fired anywhere in the process in the last 20 s (ALTO) or 45 s (MEDIO). A resident fully controls the JPEG frames sent over /ws/live for their own private camera, and each live session may emit an event every 5 s. With the committed weights, a stable person (1) loitering 15 s (2) with raised hands (3) scores 6 = ALTO, and person + loitering scores 3 = MEDIO. A resident can therefore keep both windows permanently occupied by re-sending such frames. While they are occupied, live MEDIO/ALTO events from every other user and community are still stored in the database, but they produce no siren or LED command of their own and no Telegram photo. The chat receives only the attacker's frames, so the operator never sees the victims' evidence. Without any attacker, ordinary activity in one community also silences alerts from another. The schema's per-channel min_level shows per-recipient alerting was intended.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: The alert cooldown is keyed by level alone (backend/app.py LEVEL_COOLDOWN/_last_alert), not by community, camera or recipient channel, so the shared alert budget can be used up by any principal.

candidates.title: Uploaded-video alerts bypass the live cooldown: unbounded siren commands per upload and one Telegram alert per upload
candidates.description: dispatch_alerts, called from POST /analyze, publishes one actuator command (ON:10 or WARN) for every MEDIO/ALTO event found in an uploaded video and sends one Telegram photo per upload. It has no cooldown and no per-user or per-community rate limit, and it never touches the live path's LEVEL_COOLDOWN, which exists to keep the shared channels from flooding. Any resident or community_admin can upload arbitrary video (up to MAX_UPLOAD_MB=200) against their own private camera. The event count is bounded only by video time divided by 5 s, and video time is the frame index divided by the container-declared fps, which the uploader controls. One upload can therefore yield hundreds or thousands of siren commands, keeping the shared siren on throughout dispatch. Repeated small uploads post uploader-chosen frames (any image with a detected person, red boxes added) to the shared chat as 'ALERTA DE SEGURIDAD' for the configured zone, at the upload rate instead of at most once per 20/45 s. Such bursts can hit Telegram's per-chat bot limits, and notifier failures are only logged, so other communities' alerts sent in that period may be lost. analyze is an async def handler that calls dispatch_alerts synchronously. Each event therefore also blocks the event loop for time.sleep(0.5) plus up to 5 s of wait_for_publish, stalling every other HTTP and WebSocket client during dispatch. The preceding synchronous analyze_video call is a separate /analyze resource issue owned by another unit.

candidates.title: Uploaded-video threat scoring reuses one ThreatScorer across users, so one upload changes the next user's event levels
candidates.description: GuardianEngine is a process-wide singleton. analyze_video scores every uploaded video with the single self.scorer created in __init__ and never resets it, whereas each live session gets its own ThreatScorer ('scorer propio por cliente'). ThreatScorer keeps a persistence deque and presence_start between evaluate() calls, and uploads are analysed one after another on the event loop. Say a resident's video ends with a person present who first appeared at a large video time (video time = frame index / container-declared fps, which the uploader controls). presence_start stays set. In the next uploaded video, from any user in any community, a person present from the first sampled frame then gets a negative loiter_time and loses the 2 loitering points until presence breaks. That turns person+loitering (3, MEDIO) into BAJO, so no event, siren or Telegram alert, and turns person+loitering+hands_up (6, ALTO) into MEDIO (WARN instead of siren). Conversely, a video ending with present frames makes the next video's first detection immediately 'stable'. The effect needs the attacker's upload to be analysed immediately before the victim's and affects only uploaded-video analysis, not live streams.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: engine.py analyze_video uses the engine-level self.scorer, whose temporal state (history, presence_start) persists across analyses by different users, instead of a fresh ThreatScorer per analysis as LiveSession does.

uncovered.reason: notifier.py builds the URL https://api.telegram.org/bot{token}/sendPhoto (line 59) and logs str(e) on any exception (lines 66-67, 79-80). requests connection errors embed the request path, so the bot token may be written to container logs. Secrets-in-logs is excluded from this hunter's blocks and is not covered by the git-history secrets unit.
